1:
Every voice marks the departure's finality. Henry presses the wording, that Christ did not merely go out of the temple but departed from it, taking his final farewell never to return, with the prediction of its ruin following immediately: the house Christ leaves is left desolate indeed. He adds that Christ departed not till they drove him away, and that though he left the temple he did not leave the twelve, the seed of the gospel church. Gill says it more briefly: in leaving he began to fulfil the desolation he had foretold. Robertson dates the moment: every discourse since the earlier confrontation has been inside the sacred enclosure, and now the public teaching is over, a tragic moment, with the disciples' approach an attempt to relieve the Master's thought. Ellicott prefers the reading of the best manuscripts, that Jesus departed from the Temple and was going on his way, and notes that the other evangelists attach the widow's mite to it.

Why the disciples pointed at the buildings is answered three ways. Henry takes them to have been pleased with what they showed him, men who had lived mostly in Galilee and seldom seen a structure reckoned among the wonders of the world, who expected their Master to admire it as they did. Ellicott fills in what they were looking at, the great stones, the golden and the beautiful gates, the porticos and marble cupolas and the offerings accumulated through the forty-six years since Herod began, and asks whether the sight was meant to make him recall his words of evil omen, which he thinks a far more natural account than the alternative. Calvin reads it as unbelief rather than admiration: their eyes were so dazzled by the present splendour that they could scarcely hope the kingdom of Christ would arise, and though they do not say so they tacitly suggest it by alleging all that mass against him. Barnes and Lightfoot supply the scale. Barnes cites Josephus for stones forty-five cubits long, used chiefly in the eastern wall; Lightfoot quotes the rabbinic saying that a man who never saw Herod's Temple never saw a fine building, disputes whether the marble was white and green or also spotted, and tells how the walls were built winding like waves to take plaster, which the Rabbins begged might be left as it was. Robertson calls it beautiful as a snow mountain, still unfinished.

On the stone not left upon a stone the comment turns documentary. Clarke notes that the negative is absent from several excellent manuscripts and from several versions, which read simply consider all these things, holds these to have been the last words spoken as he left the temple, and observes that from the mount where the discourse was renewed the whole city lay clearly in view. Barnes insists how improbable the thing was when said, the temple the pride of a nation then at peace, and yet accomplished exactly within forty years; he rests the proof on Josephus, a Jewish priest who fell into Roman hands and stayed through the siege, who would have said nothing designed to confirm the prophecies of Jesus, and whose history nevertheless reads almost like a running commentary on them. Ellicott adds from the same source that Titus ordered city and temple dug up, leaving two or three towers only, so that visitors could hardly believe the place inhabited, and remarks that everything recent excavation has disinterred belongs to the substructures. Wesley and Lightfoot both carry the ploughing: Wesley that the foundations were dug up after the burning and the ground ploughed, Lightfoot that the Talmudic chronicles date it to the ninth of Ab and name the general, whom he identifies with the officer Josephus says Titus left in command. Calvin gives the reason behind the sentence: God determined by this dreadful example to take vengeance on the nation for rejecting his Son.
3:
The setting is fixed first. Gill places the mount east of the city and over against the temple, where a man could take the whole of it in, and explains why the view was open: the eastern wall was built lower than the others so that the high priest, burning the red heifer here and sprinkling the blood, might see the temple gate. Robertson draws the picture of Jesus seated there looking down on the sanctuary he had just left, approached after the climb by four disciples carrying the problem his words had raised. Barnes and Ellicott both stress that the four came privately. Barnes notes the prediction had been made in the hearing of all the apostles, only a part now coming to learn when; Ellicott takes the names from the second evangelist and observes that they are the first of the three groups making up the Twelve, Andrew standing last against the pre-eminence of the other three.

How many questions were asked, and whether the askers knew what they asked, is the real matter. Barnes counts three, the date, the sign of the coming, and the sign that the age was closing, and says the reply intermingles Jerusalem's fall with that closing, so that it is sometimes hard to tell which a remark belongs to, both being describable in the same words. Clarke counts the same but reports the contrary view, that they are parts of one question and that the reply concerns only the Jewish state, nothing being said of a judgment day; he reads the phrase as the close of an economy, an accommodated use of a word whose proper force is eternal. Wesley says flatly that they inquired confusedly, as though temple and consummation were one thing, while the Lord answered distinctly, and he allots the verses accordingly: the destruction and its signs to one stretch, the coming to another, the timing of each to a third. Calvin explains how the confusion arose: believing from infancy that the temple would stand till the end of time, they could not suppose the kingdom would come while the building stood, and once told it would fall, one error leading to another, they expected to be happy the moment his reign began, left warfare out of the account, and flew at once to a triumph.

The words themselves repay attention, and two voices give it. Ellicott renders the sign of thy coming literally as of thy presence, marking it the first occurrence of a term afterwards prominent through the Epistles, and explains that in the common speech of the day, passed from the schools of the Rabbis into popular use, this age meant the time up to the Messiah and the age to come the era he was to inaugurate. Robertson adds that the same word is common in the papyri for the visit of an emperor, and refuses to say whether the disciples supposed the three events simultaneous, there being no way to answer; he grants the discourse the most difficult problem in the Synoptic Gospels, many theories of it impugning the knowledge of Jesus or of the writers or both, and is content to read the destruction that did happen in that generation as also a symbol of the coming. Clarke supports his rendering from Aristotle, that the word means continual being and no term points out eternity more forcibly. Lightfoot approaches from the other side: what the apostles meant is best conceived from what their nation expected of the Messiah's days, which he draws out of the Babylonian Sanhedrin, the tradition of the school of Elias that the righteous whom God raises shall not return to dust but live as long as God lives, with the gloss that when he renews his world he will give them wings to float upon the waters.
4:
Henry sets the terms of the whole discourse at the outset. The disciples had asked when, and to that Christ gives no answer, since it is not for us to know the times; they had also asked for a sign, and that he answers fully, because we are concerned to understand the signs of the times. The prophecy, he holds, primarily respects what lay near at hand, the destruction of Jerusalem, the end of the Jewish state, the calling of the Gentiles and the setting up of Christ's kingdom; but as the older prophecies that speak immediately of Jewish affairs look further under that figure to the gospel church, so this one, under the type of Jerusalem's ruin, looks as far as the general judgment. Calvin opens from the disciples' disappointment: they looked for a triumph as though their warfare were finished, and got an exhortation to long patience, as if told they wished to seize the prize at the outset with the course still to run, and would draw down to earth a kingdom no man obtains till he ascends to heaven.

The first sign is counterfeit Christs, and the voices differ on whether it was fulfilled; Clarke and Wesley both number it first. Robertson, taking the verb in its causative force, remarks how successful deceivers have been with their programmes, and that our word planet comes from the same root. Barnes says there is abundant evidence it was fully accomplished and sends the reader to Josephus; Clarke supplies the instances, men who claimed inspiration and led crowds into the desert promising signs of liberty, among them an Egyptian who led thirty thousand out and lost nearly all, and calls it a just judgment that a people who rejected the true Christ should be delivered to false ones. Ellicott dissents: no direct fulfilment is recorded in the New Testament or by Josephus, and the figure usually named appeared only long after Jerusalem fell, though in the fanaticism of the time such pretenders may well have risen and vanished without finding a place in history. Calvin narrows the class, treating it not as false doctrine in general but as the one sort that introduced every later error, and observing that the true Redeemer had been removed from the world and loaded with the shame of the cross while every mind was still inflamed with the desire of redemption, which gave impostors their opening.

Wars come next, and the comment turns documentary. Barnes notes that the empire was at peace when the words were spoken, and that four emperors afterwards died violently within eighteen months, factions and bloody wars following the changes of government; rumours of wars he makes wars declared or threatened but not executed. Ellicott reads the tense as a double future, confines the reference chiefly to wars affecting the Jews, and notes how aptly the historian titled his second book. Lightfoot adds the shaking of the empire under Otho, Vitellius and Vespasian, when Rome became the scene of battle and the Capitol was reduced to ashes. Robertson turns the clause into counsel: look out for the wars, but do not be terrified out of your wits, the verb meaning to be frightened by an outcry, and he remarks how readily people overlook what follows, that the end is not yet. Calvin confines these commotions to Judea, since the flame is said later to spread wider, and wants the disciples to meet them with courage, knowing none of it happened accidentally or outside God's providence. On the closing phrase four agree the word is birth-pangs: Gill and Robertson note that the Jews used the very phrase for the sufferings to precede the Messiah, Clarke makes the whole land a woman in grievous travail whose first throes these were, and Ellicott reads the world's troubles as issuing in a new birth.
9:
Gill marks the reversal: the disciples looked for a temporal kingdom and worldly grandeur, and are promised affliction, persecution and death, the Jews continuing in unbelief and delivering them to the magistrates to be scourged and imprisoned. Clarke renders the clause as a personification, that they will be delivered into affliction's own hand to be harassed by every mode of inventive torture, and takes the hatred to join Jew and Gentile, though he allows it may mean the Gentiles in particular, since the parallel accounts mention the Jewish persecution separately. Barnes documents the fulfilment from the Acts, the council before which Peter and John were brought, the synagogues and prisons and beatings, the rulers and kings; Lightfoot connects the apostolic word that judgment must begin at the house of God, reading it as notice that the time foretold had come, and describes the persecution the Jews, now near their own ruin, stirred up almost everywhere. Ellicott makes the adverb point to synchronism rather than sequence, and narrows the hatred to the heathen nations, citing how the sect was everywhere spoken against when Paul reached Rome and how a Roman historian soon described Christians as hated for their crimes.

Robertson dwells on the name rather than the suffering. He reads the periphrastic future as emphasising a continuous process, notes that the word for tribulation is the common one for the pressure Christians were under, and observes that the most glorious name in the world today was soon to be a byword of shame, which the disciples would count it an honour to bear. Wesley puts the sting in the pretext, that they would be delivered up as if they were themselves the cause of all these evils, and sharpens the universality: they would be hated even by those who tolerate every other sect and party, since in no nation will the children of the devil tolerate the children of God. Calvin treats the hatred as a distinct trial added to ordinary affliction, and states what is painful in it, that the children of God should be so treated as not to be distinguished from the despisers of God, subjected to the punishments those men endure for their crimes, and oppressed by calamities from which the ungodly go free.

The second half turns the danger inward, and the comment is nearly unanimous that the offence falls among professors. Gill describes the men who had been hearers of the apostles while things were tolerably quiet, and who stumbled at the cross once they saw apostles beaten, imprisoned and killed and the same likely to fall on themselves. Barnes makes the stumbling an apostasy which proves there was no real attachment, and the betraying a matter of securing one's own safety by revealing the names, homes or hiding-places of those who did love Christ. Clarke supplies the documentary instance, a single sentence from a Roman annalist on the persecution under Nero: at first several were seized who confessed, and by their discovery a great multitude of others were convicted and executed. Ellicott takes the stumbling-block to have been the new aspects of truth presented from time to time, the slowness of the victory, or the delay of the coming, and finds the mutual hatred fulfilled in the faction-fights at Jerusalem, the disputes between believing and unbelieving Jews city by city, and the bitterness of the Judaisers against Paul. Calvin calls this the most violent temptation of all, because it arises from bad examples, and distinguishes what it does to different men: some who had entered the right course fall away, some are exasperated against Christ, some lose all feeling of piety. Wesley reads the sequence as a charge to hold fast faith against false prophets, love when offences abound, and hope to the end, and takes the cooling of love to mean the generality of those who love God will leave their first love.
11:
The false prophets are distinguished from the false Christs already named. Calvin makes the difference explicit: there Christ spoke only of impostors who claimed the title shortly after the gospel began, while here he threatens that in every age false teachers will arise to corrupt sound doctrine, the Church under the gospel being no less exposed than it was under the Law. Barnes narrows the reference the other way, to prophets appearing during the siege itself, and quotes Josephus that the zealots who ruled the city suborned many to declare that aid would come from heaven, done to keep the people from deserting. Gill and Clarke supply names instead, teachers who pretended to a spirit of prophecy and new revelations, among them men who denied the deity or the real humanity of Christ. Ellicott gathers the New Testament witness to the same decade, the many antichrists of one apostle, the false teachers of another, the seducing spirits of a third, and reads it as the outcome of a feverish excitement among the people.

On iniquity abounding the voices divide between the public and the inward sense. Gill allows every candidate at once, the malice of persecutors, the treachery of apostates, the errors of false teachers and the plain wickedness of lives, all making up the abounding iniquity. Ellicott prefers lawlessness as the rendering and says no word could more fitly describe Judaea at that time, when brigandage, massacre, extortion and assassination became common things; he also reads the many whose love cools as the many, the greater part of the true Israel found in the Church. Barnes glosses the verb as an old word no longer used in this sense outside the Bible, and makes the fear of death and false teaching the agents that lessen ardour. Robertson presses the image in the Greek, a word for breathing cool by blowing, spiritual energy chilled by a poisonous wind, with love of the brotherhood giving way to mutual suspicion. Calvin turns it on the reader: the evil extends further than anyone observes, because the clearer the gospel light shows the malice of men, the more even well-regulated minds lose the desire to do good, each reasoning that kindness is thrown away since experience shows almost all ungrateful.

Endurance to the end is read in two senses. Clarke takes the end as the destruction of the Jewish polity and the salvation as deliverance in imminent danger, adding the remarkable fact that not a single Christian perished when Jerusalem fell. Barnes reports the same reading but thinks it more probable that final salvation is meant and the end is the close of life. Ellicott will have both: endurance to the end of life is in every case the condition of salvation, while the context points to the close of the period in view, so the promise at least includes deliverance from that destruction. On the gospel preached in all the world the comment is careful not to overstate. Ellicott insists the words must not be strained beyond what the hearers would understand, who were certain to take all the world as the Roman empire, where hardly a province had not heard the faith by then. Robertson agrees the language should not be pressed too literally and that it is not said all will be saved; Wesley says it was not universal, this not being done yet, but general through the several parts of the world, and accomplished before the city fell. Lightfoot gives the reason for the order: Jerusalem was not to be destroyed before the gospel had spread, so that the world, already a catechumen in the doctrine of Christ, might have an undeniable testimony in the vengeance poured out on that city. Calvin adds that the promise was given to raise minds that were cast down, the apostles being bound to cherish hope against hope.
15:
The phrase is traced to Daniel by every voice, and translated variously. Barnes calls it a Hebrew expression meaning an abominable or hateful destroyer. Wesley gives Daniel's form as the abomination that maketh desolate and identifies it with the standards of the desolating legions, which bore the abominable images of their idols. Lightfoot renders the Daniel verse himself, that in the middle of the last week the sacrifice and oblation would cease, even until the wing or army of abomination should make desolate. Robertson notes that the verb behind the noun means to feel nausea at a stench, and recalls that Antiochus had erected an altar to Zeus on the altar of Jehovah, which is the desecration Daniel's words first described. Ellicott takes that earlier desecration as the plain sense in Daniel, the mad attempt to stop the daily sacrifice and substitute an idolatrous worship, and treats the question of what analogous thing our Lord meant as one that has received very different answers.

Most of the voices answer it the same way. Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and Robertson follow the third evangelist in making the abomination the Roman army, and all explain the name by the ensigns: the images of the emperor and the eagles were carried before the legions and given divine honours, so the army was an abomination to Jewish eyes. Clarke and Robertson add the same report from Josephus, that the Romans brought their ensigns into the temple, set them over against the eastern gate and sacrificed to them there. Wesley widens the holy place beyond the temple and its mountain to the whole city and several furlongs about it, including the very mount where the discourse was delivered and where the Romans later planted those ensigns. Barnes notes that the second evangelist says simply standing where it ought not, and that all Jerusalem was esteemed holy. Gill clears away the wrong candidates instead of naming the right one: not a statue set up by the Romans, not the golden eagle Herod placed on the temple gate, which came before these words, not the image of Tiberius said to have been brought in by Pilate, too near at hand for a prophecy, and least of all the statue of Adrian, which stood there more than a hundred and thirty years after the city fell.

Ellicott alone refuses the consensus, and does it on two grounds. The warning is given before the Temple's destruction, so the abomination cannot be the plundering troops or the eagles inside it; and it is said to stand in the Holy Place, so neither can it be the eagles in the besieging lines of the earlier general. He looks for the answer rather in the faction-fights within the city, the murders and outrages and the profanations committed there by the Jews themselves. On the parenthesis that follows, Lightfoot holds it was spoken not for the obscurity of the prophecy but for its certainty: whoever reads those words should mind well that when the army of the prince to come compasses Jerusalem with a siege, destruction is certain. Robertson observes that the same aside stands in the second gospel and doubts that Jesus spoke the words himself. Calvin supplies the reason the prophet is cited at all. The overthrow of temple, city and government was incredible, and it might well seem strange that the disciples could not be saved without being torn from the nation to which the covenants of eternal salvation had been committed; so Christ confirms both points from Daniel, as if to say that they must not be too strongly attached to the temple and the ceremonies of the Law, since God had limited them to a fixed time and had long ago declared that when the Redeemer came the sacrifices would cease.
16:
The command to flee is reported as a warning that was actually obeyed. Clarke says the counsel was remembered and wisely followed, and cites the early historians that when the first siege was raised and a second army approached, all who believed in Christ left Jerusalem for Pella and other places beyond Jordan, so that not one of them perished. Ellicott gives the same account more precisely, that the Christians of Judaea acted on a certain oracle and fled to a town on the northern boundary beyond Jordan, and adds from Josephus that many of the more conspicuous citizens left the city as men abandon a sinking ship. Robertson places Pella at the foot of the mountains east of the Jordan and says simply that they remembered the warning and fled for safety; Wesley adds the detail that made the signal legible, the unexpected and impolitic withdrawal of the Romans after their first advance, which the Christians took as their cue to retire, some to Pella and others to Mount Libanus. Gill reads the direction as telling those in the city and in the towns of Judaea alike not to shelter in Jerusalem on the strength of its fortifications but to flee elsewhere. Barnes explains why the mountains: the hills of Palestine abound in caves, which were in every age the haunt of robbers and the refuge of men pursued. Calvin draws the inference that governs the whole passage, that once the temple was profaned the services of the Law would soon be abolished, so that nothing would be more desirable than distance from the place, and that the calamities would come so suddenly as scarcely to leave time for the most rapid flight.

The two illustrations of haste turn on how the houses were built. Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all explain that the roofs were flat and used for walking, for retirement, for conversation and even for prayer and preaching, and that stairs ran up the outside so that a man could go up or come down without entering the house. Clarke and Ellicott add what makes the picture work: in the walled cities the flat roofs formed a continuous terrace from one end to the other, ending at the gates, so that a man might pass from house to house without descending into the street until he reached a point near the wall and could escape. Robertson gives the rabbinic name for it, the road of the roofs, and says there was need for haste. Barnes draws the moral that the man on the roof should not stop even to secure a garment from inside, since the delay would endanger his life. Wesley notes only that the stairs were on the outside. On the man in the field the comment is narrower. Gill has him at the plough or the sowing or some other rural business; Ellicott corrects the plural to a singular cloak and explains that the labourer worked in the short tunic and left the flowing outer garment at home in the city, so that going back for it meant going back into danger; Robertson says the same of the peasant's mantle. Clarke supplies the reason the warning is absolute: once the Roman army sat down before the city there would be no further possibility of escape, since they would never move until Jerusalem was destroyed.
19:
The woe on the pregnant is read as pity, not blame. Gill is careful that it is no crime nor judgment to be with child, fruitfulness having always been reckoned a blessing, and that what is meant is the misery of women who by reason of their burden could not flee speedily and must stay and endure the siege. Ellicott prefers alas for them to woe unto them and says the tone is pity rather than denunciation, the hardships of a hurried flight pressing most on those encumbered with infants or expecting childbirth, the same tenderness showing in the words later spoken to the daughters of Jerusalem. Both think the phrase points further, to the horrors of the siege itself, when the houses were full of women and children who perished by famine and mothers snatched food from their own children's mouths.

On the prayer about the season the voices agree on the principle. Barnes draws out the logic: the destruction was coming and could not be prevented, yet it was right to pray that its circumstances be mitigated, as it is right for us to pray that calamities we know must come may come as mildly as is consistent with God's will. Gill lists what makes winter flight hard: short days, roads sometimes made impassable by snow or flood, and the comfortlessness of lodging in mountains. Clarke gives the same reasons and reports the rabbinic observation, which Lightfoot supplies at greater length, that God showed particular favour in the destruction of the first temple by not obliging the Jews to go out in winter. Ellicott explains the structure of the saying, that rules were given for what lay within their power while what lay outside their will might lawfully be prayed about, and notes that the first evangelist alone records the clause about the sabbath, writing for Jews whose strict observance would hinder them by their own scruples from going beyond a sabbath day's journey. Robertson says the same more shortly, and Wesley adds that the Jews thought it unlawful to walk above two thousand paces on that day, and that in the event the flight fell in the spring.

The tribulation itself is measured against all history. Ellicott traces the superlative to Daniel and says a reader of Josephus will hardly hesitate to adopt the historian's own language, that all the miseries known from the beginning of the world fell short of those of the siege; other sieges may have shown wretchedness as appalling, but nothing history records offers a parallel. Clarke says no history can furnish one, rapine, murder, famine and pestilence within and fire and sword without, and observes that our Lord wept at the foresight of it and that it is almost impossible to read the account without weeping too. Barnes takes its content from the third evangelist, the falling by the sword, the captivity among all nations, and Jerusalem trodden down until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Calvin looks past the physical to the most destructive plague of all, that the light of heavenly doctrine was extinguished among them and they were rejected by God. On the shortening of the days the question is for whose sake. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley answer that the elect are the Christians, and that without the shortening the whole nation would have been destroyed; Clarke puts the number who perished at eleven hundred thousand and says the nation would soon have been extirpated. Robertson treats the past tense as a prophetic figure, the future regarded as past, and lists the accidents that actually shortened the siege. Lightfoot states the symmetry he finds in it, that God lengthened the time for the sake of the elect before the destruction and shortened it for their sake in the destruction. Calvin sets the promise beside the prophet's small seed, without which the people would have been as Sodom.
23:
The warning against false Christs is repeated, and the voices ask why. Calvin answers that the danger was great, since men whose affairs were desperate would be deceived by false pretences, seeking phantoms instead of Christ and embracing Satan's delusions as though they were help from God. Clarke notes the caution had been given already but holds there would be special need of it about the siege, and that the lower the Jews were reduced the readier they were to listen. Barnes explains the appetite: the Messiah was expected to deliver them from Rome, so in great calamities they would look for him anxiously, and many would rejoice to believe he had come and call on others, Christians among them, to follow. Gill places the cry at any of three moments, when the siege began, while it lasted, or after the city fell and men scattered in the country told their countrymen the Messiah was in such a place. Ellicott notes that Josephus, while speaking of many deceivers claiming divine authority, says nothing of pretenders to the Messiah's character, and suspects the silence was a suppression of the truth connected with his own recognition of Vespasian.

On the signs and wonders the comment is partly lexical and partly historical. Robertson separates the three words the New Testament uses of such works, the prodigy, the mighty power and the sign of God's purpose, noting that our word miracle carries only one of those notions. Barnes takes the showing of signs to mean pretending to work miracles, so nearly resembling true prophets in miraculous power as to make the imposture hard to detect. Ellicott offers two instances from the Acts as representative claimants to supernatural powers, connects the signs and lying wonders foretold of the Wicked One, and adds that but for this warning even the elect, the Christians of Judaea, might have been carried away by popular delusion. Lightfoot turns to the credulity that made it possible, asking whether the nation was madder in its religious superstition or its taste for curious arts, and reporting how much they attributed to dreams, even imposing fasts to obtain a happy one or turn aside the ill omen of another. Wesley takes the saving clause as decisive: they would deceive the elect if it were possible, but it is not possible that God should suffer the body of Christians to be so deceived. Calvin reads it as meant to excite alarm and keep believers watchful, while reminding them not to be troubled at the strangeness of the sight.

The forewarning is then pressed as a duty. Gill takes it as notice given before the events, so the disciples would be inexcusable if not on their guard, and adds that the fulfilment would afterwards serve as an argument for Christ against these pretenders. Calvin draws the sharper inference, that those dismayed by the stumbling-blocks Christ predicted are inexcusable, since timely warning that such is God's pleasure ought to be enough; and he adds that God is faithful and will not suffer us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. On the places where the pretender would be sought, Barnes explains that the Jews expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from some unexpected quarter, so that most of the impostors led their people into the deserts. Clarke remarks that our Lord foretold not only the appearance of these men but the manner of their conduct, and confirms the desert from Josephus, who tells of impostors persuading the people to follow them there with promises of signs and wonders. Ellicott glosses the secret chambers as the closet of an earlier chapter and explains that the pretenders would shun the publicity which would test their claims, so rumours would be whispered of a Christ concealed beyond the Jordan or in some zealot's house, to appear at the last moment and claim the throne of David.
27:
The lightning is taken by nearly every voice as a figure of manner rather than of direction. Barnes says plainly that it is not designed to denote the quarter from which he will come but the way of it, rapid and unexpected, so that looking for him in the desert or in secret places is useless. Robertson sets the visibility of the flash against the invisibility of the false Messiahs. Wesley makes the point about timing, that the coming will be as quick as lightning, leaving no room for any previous warning of the kind the pretenders offer. Clarke alone presses the compass points as significant, finding in them the very march of the Roman army, which entered Judaea from the east and carried its conquest westward, so that the extent of the ruin and the route of the army are both in the comparison. Ellicott steps back to say where the reader now stands: in these verses we are on the dim border-land between the primary and the ultimate fulfilments, since the disciples had themselves joined the destruction of Jerusalem to the coming of their Lord, and the two are joined in his own words as well. Lightfoot supplies the principle that makes such doubleness readable, that the destruction of Jerusalem is very frequently expressed in Scripture as though it were the destruction of the whole world, and he cites the song of Moses on a fire kindled in God's anger burning to the lowest hell, where the subject is the wrath consuming that people.

The proverb of the carcass and the eagles divides the voices sharply. Clarke, Lightfoot, Barnes and Wesley all read it of Jerusalem and the legions. Clarke makes the carcass the Jewish nation, morally and judicially dead, and the eagles the Roman armies, so called partly for their strength and fierceness and partly for the figure wrought on their ensigns, remarking that the Roman fury pursued these men wherever they were found. Lightfoot says he wonders that anyone can understand the words of pious men flying to Christ when the discourse is of quite another thing, and gives the connection: when God casts off a city grown ripe for destruction, like a carcass thrown out, the soldiers will fly to it with their eagles to tear and devour. Barnes calls the words proverbial, since vultures and eagles find dead bodies easily, and adds that the proverb teaches a universal truth as well. Wesley makes it a further reason for not listening to any pretended deliverer: expect no deliverer of the Jewish nation, for it is already before God a dead carcass which the Roman eagles will soon devour. Gill reaches the same identification by first refusing the alternative, that the carcass is Christ crucified, to whom the word will by no means agree. Ellicott rejects two readings at once, the one that finds the legions and a corrupt Judaism in the figure, which he grants true as far as it goes but calls too narrow for so wide a comparison, and what he describes as the strange fantastic imagination of many of the Fathers about the carcass. Robertson adds that the bird may be the griffon vulture rather than the eagle, larger than the eagle and often seen in the wake of an army, and sets the proverb beside the like sayings in Job and the Proverbs. Calvin takes it quite differently again, as a figure of union: by whatever methods Satan tries to scatter the children of God, in Christ himself is the sacred bond by which they are kept together, since dispersion comes of departing from him in whom alone our strength lies.
29:
This verse divides the commentators more than any other in the chapter, and the word immediately is what divides them. Gill takes it strictly: what follows comes to pass just upon the destruction of the city and the temple, and therefore cannot be referred to the last judgment, nor to the church, nor to the whole intervening time. Clarke agrees and says why the common reading is wrong: commentators generally understand this of the end of the world and the coming to judgment, but the word immediately shows that our Lord is not speaking of a distant event but of something consequent on calamities already predicted, which can only be the destruction of Jerusalem. Lightfoot supplies the figure both rely on, that the Jewish heaven shall perish and the sun and moon of its glory be darkened, the sun being the religion of the church, the moon the government of the state, and the stars the judges and doctors of both. Barnes argues the same point from usage rather than from the adverb: the images are not to be taken literally, the sacred writers employing the darkening of sun and moon and the falling of stars for any great calamity, the overturning of kingdoms or the dethroning of princes, as the fall of Babylon is foretold in just these terms.

Three voices read it the other way. Ellicott holds that from this point the prophecy takes a wider range and passes beyond the narrow limits of Jerusalem to the final coming of the Son of Man, the one represented as following immediately on the other, and insists that no other meaning could have been found in the words when they were first heard or read, the days being those shortened for the elect's sake and the tribulation the one already named. Wesley says flatly that here our Lord begins to speak of his last coming, and resolves the adverb by the speaker rather than the event: he speaks not so much in the language of man as of God, with whom a thousand years are as one day, and many of the primitive Christians, not observing this, thought he would come immediately in the common sense of the word, a mistake which Paul labours to remove in his second letter to the Thessalonians. Henry takes the same side and offers the same kind of defence, that it is usual for prophets to speak of things as near and just at hand in order to express their greatness and certainty, and reads the whole as foretelling a great change in order to the making of all things new.

Two voices decline the choice. Robertson grants that the adverb gives trouble if one stresses the time element, and asks how much time intervenes between the tribulation of those days and the symbolism that follows; he points to the comparable language of the Apocalypse as a reason to pause before deciding, calls what we have here a prophetic panorama with foreshortened perspective, asks for sobriety of judgment about such apocalyptic pictures, and says that literalism will not serve. Calvin treats the verse as the turn to the full manifestation of the kingdom, which is what the disciples had asked about in the first place, and makes the promise that after they have been tried by so many distressing events the redemption will arrive in due time; the principal object of the reply, he says, was to confirm them in good hope so that they might not be dismayed by the confusion that would arise, and for that reason Christ does not speak in simple terms but in the modes of expression common among the prophets. Henry adds the contrast that holds for either reading: at his first coming Christ was set for a sign to be spoken against, and at his second he will be a sign to be admired.
30:
What the sign of the Son of man is nobody claims to know. Ellicott asks outright whether we can picture it and whether it is distinct from the coming so closely joined to it, and reports wildly conjectural answers, a cross in the sky as though Constantine's vision were reproduced, a lightning flash dazzling all men, or some manifestation none can imagine beforehand. Gill clears the ground the same way, refusing the trumpet of the next verse, the clouds of this one, and that cross in the air, his reason against the trumpet being that this sign is not said to be sounded but to appear. Robertson prefers the suggestion that Christ himself is the sign, taking the genitive as one of apposition, which he finds confirmed by the rest of the verse, that they shall see the Son of man coming. Wesley alone ventures a guess: the sign appears a little before he descends, the heavenly bodies being extinguished, and is perhaps the cross.

Those who read the passage of Jerusalem give the sign a different content. Clarke makes the plain meaning this, that the destruction of the city will be so signal a manifestation of Christ's power that all the Jewish tribes shall mourn and many be led to acknowledge him, and he takes the word rendered earth to mean the land of Judaea. Lightfoot puts it as a proof of identity: the Son of man gives proof of himself whom they would not acknowledge, not in any visible figure but in vengeance so visible that the tribes must own him the avenger, for many times they asked a sign and now a sign shall appear. Barnes allows both at once, taking the sign as evidence that Christ is coming to destroy the city while not denying that it applies also to the day of judgment, since the disciples had asked about both. Calvin uses the term to mark the difference between the present condition of Christ's kingdom and its future glory, admitting that amid the confused mixture of things we now perceive his majesty does not fully appear and the redemption he brought is buried almost out of sight.

On the angels and the trumpet the division runs along the same line. Clarke and Gill make the angels messengers rather than spirits, the apostles and their successors, sent into the world of the Gentiles to preach once the church at Jerusalem was dissolved; Clarke reads the trumpet as the earnest call of the gospel and the elect as the Gentiles now chosen in place of the rebellious Jews. Lightfoot gives the same sequence: when Jerusalem is ashes the Son of man sends his ministers with the trumpet of the gospel to gather his elect out of the nations, so that God shall not want a church. Barnes notes the word means literally messengers and is applied even to inanimate things God employs, though it most commonly means the exalted intelligences, and allows either sense. Against them Robertson holds the coming is clearly not to be identified with the judgment of Jerusalem but forms its preternatural background, and places the trumpet among the standing images of prophecy, the signal that called Israel to march. Ellicott marks the verse as the formal expansion of what two earlier parables hinted, prefers the manuscripts which omit the word sound, and admits we cannot know what reality will answer to the symbol, though it is worth noting how deeply it impressed those who heard it. Calvin reads the gathering from the four winds as hyperbole, to show that even if the elect were scattered in the air they would be united under their head, Christ consoling disciples who might be discouraged by the Church's dispersion. Wesley defines the elect simply as all who have endured to the end in the faith which works by love.
32:
The fig tree is an argument about reading signs. Henry makes it the practical application of the whole prediction, that we must expect these events and prepare for them, observing the signs of the times and comparing them with the word so as to foresee what is at the door; the parable itself is no more than that budding and blossoming presage summer. Clarke puts the same thing as a proof: the signs given will be as infallible evidence of the approaching ruin of the Jewish state as the budding of the trees is of the coming summer. Gill and Barnes supply the natural detail, Gill that the tree was well known in Judaea and its putting forth fell under everyone's observation, Barnes that the word means an illustration and that the juices return from the roots so the buds swell and burst. Both think a fig tree may have been in sight, since the discourse was on the Mount of Olives where figs grew as well as olives, and Ellicott adds that the season was early spring. Calvin refuses the obvious reading: not merely that the coming will be as evident a sign as greenness is of summer, but a comparison drawn from the way trees contracted by winter show greater vigour afterwards.

On this generation the chapter's sharpest textual disagreement appears. Clarke renders it this race and argues that the Jews shall not cease from being a distinct people till all the counsels of God concerning them and the Gentiles are fulfilled, allowing that others translate it of the persons then living. Every other voice takes the ordinary sense. Barnes makes a generation thirty or forty years, and the destruction came about forty years after. Ellicott says the natural meaning is beyond question the one that takes the word for those then living, and ascribes the other rendering to a desire to bring the words into apparent harmony with history. Lightfoot draws his inference from it, that the foregoing verses cannot be of the last judgment but of the destruction of Jerusalem, since some disciples lived to see these things and some rabbis then alive survived the city's fall. Wesley reads it as implying that a great part of that generation would be passed away but not the whole, and observes it fell out just so, the city being destroyed thirty-nine or forty years later. Robertson says that if the reference is to the destruction of Jerusalem there was a literal fulfilment, taking the words in the same sense as in the verse before. Calvin holds that Christ does not extend the discourse to all the miseries that would befall the Church but tells them they will learn his words true before a single generation is completed, the city being destroyed and the temple razed within fifty years.

The saying about heaven and earth is read as a claim rather than a prediction. Ellicott hears the tone of one speaking with supreme authority, foreseeing death and seeming failure on the one hand and ultimate victory on the other, not of truth in the abstract but of his own word as the truth: the Son of Man claims for his words the eternity belonging to the words of Jehovah. Barnes puts it as a comparison: one may sooner expect heaven and earth to return to nothing than these words to fail. Calvin says he illustrates their certainty by making them more stable than the entire structure of the world, and notes that commentators explain the expression variously. Gill alone takes the first clause as an assertion about the end of time, and qualifies it: not as to the substance of the heavens and earth, which will always remain, but as to their qualities, so that they are renewed and refined rather than destroyed, the evil circumstances attending them through man's sin passing away while they continue.
36:
Whose day is unknown is disputed first. Gill restricts it: not the second coming and the last judgment, but the coming of the Son of man to take vengeance on the Jews, since the words concern the date of the things already described. Clarke supports a like reading by translating the second noun as season rather than hour, a sense he says both sacred and profane authors use, and argues it from the earlier directions: because the day was unknown they were to pray it might not fall on a sabbath, and because the season was unknown that it might not be in winter. Robertson takes the other side: it is equally clear that here Jesus has in mind his second coming, having stated plainly that the destruction of Jerusalem would happen in that generation and stating now as pointedly that no one knows this day. Wesley agrees that the day of judgment is meant and adds a careful qualification, that no man knew it while our Lord was on earth, though it might afterwards be revealed to John consistently with this. Ellicott fastens on the second evangelist's addition, neither the Son, or better not even the Son, which he calls every way remarkable and explains by that Gospel's connection with Peter, as if the apostle who heard the discourse wished to put his Master's very words on record.

Robertson treats the same clause as probably genuine here too, the idea being involved in the words but the Father only. Barnes keeps to the structure of the answer: the general signs have been given, as budding indicates summer, but the precise time is not indicated by them, and to that part of the question the reply is that it would not be foretold. Calvin states the purpose of the ignorance: Christ held believers' minds in suspense so that they might not by a false imagination fix any time for the final redemption, knowing how fickle our minds are and how a vain curiosity tickles us to know more than is proper, and perceiving the disciples' haste for a triumph.

The days of Noah are then taken as a figure of unpreparedness rather than of wickedness. Barnes sets out two points of likeness: the coming would be sudden and unexpected though general indications were given, and the world would be found as it was then. Gill reads it both ways, that the practices of that generation will be those of the age in which the Son of man comes, and that the flood fell suddenly on men thoughtless about it although warned. Robertson makes the contrast sharply: in Noah's day there was plenty of warning but utter unpreparedness, and most people are either indifferent about the second coming or have fanciful schemes about it, few being really expectant and leaving the time to God. Clarke takes the eating and drinking to mean they spent their time in rapine, luxury and riot, and says the design of the verses is that the desolation should be as general as it was unexpected. Both press the point that they had notice and would not take it, Gill that they slighted Noah's warnings and were given up to judicial blindness, Clarke that they did not lay it to heart till too late. Ellicott turns the verse back on the earlier dispute: this reckless apathy justifies reading the signs of the Advent not as phenomena visible to the eye of sense, which would make such unconcern impossible, but as signs of the times discerned only by the insight of the faithful. Calvin finds the cause of the ignorance in unbelief, which blinded their minds, where by contrast Noah beheld at a distance the vengeance still concealed and feared it early. Lightfoot notes that Peter sets the ruin of the old world and of Jerusalem side by side as parallels.
40:
Whether being taken is mercy or ruin the voices cannot settle. Ellicott states the difficulty exactly: the present tense expresses the certainty of the future, one is taken and one is left, and the form leaves it uncertain which alternative belongs to the chosen, whether the man taken is received into fellowship with Christ or carried away in judgment. Barnes allows both senses of the word, to be taken away from the danger and rescued, or to be taken away by death, and thinks the latter probably meant. Wesley takes the opposite view without hesitation, that the one is taken into God's immediate protection and the other left to share the common calamities, and remarks that our Lord speaks as having the whole transaction present before his eyes. Clarke reads the pair of illustrations as a measure of how general the calamity would be, no two persons anywhere being both able to escape, captivity and the sword having a complete triumph over that unhappy people.

The grinding at the mill is explained as the lowest kind of labour. Barnes describes the stones, two feet across and half a foot thick, the lower fixed and the upper turned by a handle, worked by two persons sitting opposite. Ellicott gives the same picture of the hand-mill, one woman holding the lower stone while another turns the upper, and notes that elsewhere the employment appears as the crowning degradation of captives taken in battle. Gill observes that the word women is not in the Greek but is rightly supplied, the participle being feminine and the work belonging to women; Robertson prefers the reading mill to millhouse and locates the handle near the edge of the upper stone.

The charge to watch is then pressed by everyone. Gill draws it as an inference from what precedes rather than a new subject, the time of the desolation being uncertain and coming on the Jews unawares. Robertson glosses the imperative as keep awake, be on the watch, and notes that Jesus enforces the point with half a dozen parables that follow. Clarke puts the historical result bluntly: this advice the followers of Christ took and therefore escaped, while the miserable Jews rejected it and were destroyed. Henry defines the watching inwardly, as maintaining the temper of mind we would be willing for our Lord to find us in, since we know we have but a little time to live and cannot know we have a long time, much less the time fixed for the judgment. Calvin takes the more pointed form of the exhortation in the third Gospel: a man whose senses are overloaded with food and wine will never raise his mind to the heavenly life, and since no desire of the flesh fails to intoxicate, they must not satiate themselves with the world. Wesley reads the uncertainty two ways at once, that the Lord may come either to require a man's soul of him or to avenge himself of that nation. On the thief the comment converges. Barnes and Clarke both put the householder's case, that a man who knew the hour would be ready, so not knowing it he must keep always watchful; Robertson notes that the breaking through is digging through a tile roof or under a floor of beaten earth. Ellicott observes that these verses have no counterpart in the other reports but stand almost word for word in another discourse, so one must choose between a repetition and a transfer of what was spoken elsewhere. Gill makes the readiness the point rather than the figure, and Ellicott concludes that even the signs likened to the budding fig were meant only to rouse the faithful, not to let men fix times the Father has kept in his own power.
45:
The question is read as pointed at the hearers rather than asked in the air. Gill notes the Latin adds do you think, and takes it as a question put to the disciples to apply to themselves, observing that in the other Gospel it answers Peter's question whether the exhortation was for them or for all, which makes it look particularly designed for them. Calvin explains that occasion: Christ having said the suddenness of his coming left no room for sloth, Peter asked whether the doctrine was general or belonged to the twelve alone, the disciples being always apt to think themselves unjustly treated unless given some distinction. Barnes observes that the passage is a parable though not expressly called one, designed to show that the disciples should act as if each moment expecting their Lord's return, illustrated by a servant who did not expect his master soon.

On the two adjectives the comment turns moral. Ellicott prefers the definite article, who then is the faithful and wise servant, and explains that the second word is the one ethical writers used for the moral wisdom which adapts means to ends, against the wisdom of contemplation on one side or technical skill on the other. Wesley makes both words a question to the reader, which of you aspires after this character, and defines them: wise, in retaining every moment the clearest conviction that all he now has is only entrusted to him as a steward, and faithful, in thinking and speaking and acting continually in a manner suitable to that conviction. Clarke reads the whole as an abstract of a minister's duties, holding that all should live in the same expectation of Christ's coming that a servant has of his master's return, having to give an exact account of the affairs left in his hands. Ellicott corrects the rendering of the servant's task, that it is to give them their food rather than meat in due season.

The blessing and the reward are read at more than one level. Gill allows three comings at which the servant might be found so doing, in judgment against Jerusalem, at death when his Lord removes him out of time, or at the day of judgment when the righteous judge gives him the crown. Clarke reduces the blessedness to one thing, that it consists in his master's approbation. Ellicott grants that the words in their letter seem to refer only to those found watching at the final advent, but says Christian insight has rightly widened them, since as there are days of the Lord in the history of churches and nations, so the Lord comes to men in the crises of their own lives. Gill treats the solemn preface as a guarantee, that nothing is a greater truth or more to be depended on, and that all such diligent servants may expect it. On the promotion Barnes is careful to say what it does not mean: the setting of the servant over all the property is a circumstance of the story designed to show the effect of faithfulness, and does not mean that ministers shall have higher rank, the reward being God's approbation. Clarke takes it as a heavenly privilege of the faithful minister, who receives power to dispense all the blessings of the new covenant with his word accompanied by the demonstration of the Spirit, and warns that much of a preacher's usefulness may be lost by unfaithfulness. Ellicott finds in the words an indication that the work of the faithful servant does not cease either after his removal from earthly labour or even after the final consummation of the kingdom, since over and above the beatific vision there will still be a work to be done.
48:
The evil servant is defined by what he says in his heart. Barnes glosses the clause as a secret supposition that the master will not return for a long time, or perhaps not at all. Gill allows that such a man may have gifts and hold the highest post in the church, graceless men being sometimes in such places, while destitute of the grace of God. Wesley marks the tense, that he is now evil, having put away faith and a good conscience. Robertson names the temptation that follows, to indulge fleshly appetites or the pride of superior intellect, and observes that within a generation scoffers would ask where the promise of the coming was, forgetting that God's clock is not like ours. Ellicott finds the temper identical with one the apostle describes, and calls the words memorable as implying foreknowledge, amid words that indicate nearness, that there would be what men would take for delay. Calvin states it as a diagnosis: this is the source of the carelessness that creeps on wicked servants, that they trust to a longer delay and involve themselves in darkness of their own accord, imagining the day of account will never come and promising themselves impunity.

Clarke orders the whole passage into a scheme, finding three characters of a bad minister and three punishments to answer them. The first is that he has little or no faith in the speedy coming of Christ, which he may not profess outwardly but says in his heart, so teaching what he does not believe; the second is that he governs with absolute dominion, oppressing his colleagues. Gill describes that oppression in detail, the abuse of power lodged in him, the usurping of dominion over the faith of others, the imposing on consciences of what Christ never commanded, the burdening with trifling rites, and the persecuting of saints who will not come into his way of believing. Barnes makes the same point more briefly, that the conduct is designed to represent ministers who are unfaithful and overbearing and abuse their trust in the church. Clarke's punishments answer his characters: a sudden death with the weight of God's judgments falling before a moment can avert it, answering the man's forgetfulness, and a separation from the communion of saints and from the gifts he has abused, answering the abuse of his authority.

The sentence itself is read as figure rather than as practice, though the practice is documented. Barnes says the punishment was anciently inflicted, sometimes by the sword and sometimes by saws, among the Chaldeans and Hebrews as well as the Egyptians and Romans, but holds it is perhaps not literal here and signifies only that the servant should be severely punished. Clarke assembles the evidence from the historians, including the report that Isaiah was sawn asunder and instances of kings who ordered men cut in two. Gill offers a different reading, the separating of soul and body by death, the taking away of his gifts, and his removal from office and from the communion of saints, and reports the suggestion that the allusion is to the cutting up of sacrifices. Ellicott takes the form of punishment to have been chosen for its figurative fitness rather than its literal sense: the man had been double-minded, trying to serve two masters, and his Lord with the sharp sword of judgment smites through the false apparent unity of his life and reveals its duplicity. On the portion with the hypocrites Barnes notes they are spoken of as the worst of offenders, and Wesley presses the propriety of the word if ministers are meant, since no hypocrisy can be baser than to call ourselves ministers of Christ while slaves of avarice, ambition or sensuality, with the prayer that God would reform them or disarm them of the influence they abuse.
